ENDOCRINOLOGY #1

TOPICS #2

  • Regulation of hormone secretion
  • • Feedback control
  • Primary and secondary endocrine dysfunction
  • 2. The endocrine hypothalamus, hypotalamic-hypophysial-portal system
  • 3. Growth and puberty
  • Normal puberty
  • Delayed / premature (precocious) puberty
  • 4. Pituitary Gland: Location and Function
  • Disorders
  • The pituitary tumoral syndrome
  • 5. Diabetes insipidus (DI)

Slide 3 #3

  • Hormones = signaling molecules that traffic information from one cell to another, typically through a soluble medium like the extracellular fluid.
  • The endocrine glands: pituitary gland, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal gland, ovary/ testis, the pineal gland (secretes melatonin), thymus, endocrine pancreas
  • nontraditional endocrine organs: gastrointestinal tract (→gastrina, VIP), NS (→noradrenalina), heart (→atrial natriuretic factor), adipose tissue (→leptina, adiponectina)

Regulation of hormone levels and feedback #4

  • Hormone levels →modulated through regulatory factors affecting several steps.
  • Many, if not most, hormone levels are controlled either directly or indirectly by the biologic activity that they serve to control.
  • Most endocrine glands are under the control of negative feedback mechanisms
  • (NEGATIVE FEEDBACK).
  • For example, PTH secretion ← to ↓ extracellular calcium levels, mobilizes calcium out of bone which, in turn, signals back to the parathyroid gland to turn off additional PTH secretion.
  • This negative feed back loop is a hallmark of endocrine regulation.

Examples of negative feedback #5

The end product or negative regulator can either be an #6

  • an inorganic ion or metabolite (eg, calcium for PTH) or
  • a hormonal product in the endocrine cascade (eg, thyroid hormone for TSH, cortisol for ACTH, IGF-1 for GH).
  • Many hormones are linked to the HP-axis. The hypothalamus modulates hypophysis function and consequently, hormones that are produced in the pituitary gland (ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH) ↑production of hormones in peripheral glands (cortisol,T3, T4,testosterone/estradiol).

REGULATION OF THE ES = NEGATIV feedback (FB) (inverse connectivity ) #7

  • Production of H and P hormones is subject to negative regulation by peripheral hormones in classic FB loops.
  • Long FB
  • Short FB
  • Ultrashort FB
  • CRH
  • ACTH
  • Cortizol
  • An example of the negative feedback system in the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis is demonstrated in Fig.

Not all feedback is negative in nature. #8

  • Positive feedback loops (eg, mid-cycle estradiol-induced LH secretion ) also play a important roles in governing physiological homeostasis.

Etiopathogeny of the endocrine disorders #9

  • HPT
  • HPT
  • HPT
  • HPF
  • HPF
  • HPF
  • Target Gland
  • TG
  • R
  • CENTRAL ED
  • PRIMARY ED
  • RECEPTOR ED
  • SECONDARY ED
  • ‘Primary’ gland failure due to a disease process in the endocrine end-organ (thyroid, adrenal or gonad) will lead to the deficiency of the hormone produced by that gland and a loss of negative feedback and subsequent elevation in the corresponding anterior pituitary hormone.
  • In ‘secondary gland failure’, there are low or ‘inappropriately normal’ levels of the pituitary trophic hormone in the face of a low end-organ hormone level. For example, if a patient has low circulating fT3 and fT4 levels in the context of a low TSH, pituitary disease should be suspected.

Etiopathogeny of the endocrine disorders #10

  • HPT
  • HPT
  • HPT
  • HPF
  • HPF
  • HPF
  • Target Gland
  • TG
  • Rec
  • CENTRAL ED
  • PRIMARY ED
  • RECEPTOR ED
  • SECONDARY ED
  • Particular types of endocrine disorder are hormone –resistance syndromes ( eg, steroid, androgen or thyroid hormone receptor resistance syndromes).
  • ⇒ characterized by a clinical phenotype suggesting hormone deficiency, by ↑levels of circulating hormone ligand (cortisol, testosterone, T3) and ↑ (or inappropriately detectable) levels of the relevant trophic regulatory hormone (e.g., ACTH, LH, TSH.)
  • Thus, if androgen receptors are defective, normal levels of androgen will not produce masculinization (e.g. androgen insensitivity syndrome).
  • Target Gland

HYPOTHALAMUS and PITUITARY GLAND #11

The pituitary stalk-the hypothalamic-hypophysial-portal system → The hypothalamus is anatomically and functionally related to the pituitary gland (hypophysis) by the infundibulum (or pituitary stalk), which consists of hypophysial portal system and also carries axons of neurons whose cell bodies reside in the SON and PVN of the HPT, respectively. #12

Endocrine Hypothalamus #13

  • NEUROHORMONES (Post Pituitary H)
  • Vasopressin (ADH)
  • Oxytocin
  • (they are nonapeptides)
  • They are synthesized in magnocellular neurons in the SON and PVN. The neurosecretory granules with ADH and OC travel down the long axons through the stalk to the Post HPF where the granules are stored and then released into the general circulation.
  • HYPOPHYSIOTROPIC H. (releasing hormones and inhibiting hormones, reflecting their influence on anterior pituitary hormones)
  • GnRH
  • GHRH, somatostatin (SS )
  • TRH
  • CRH
  • DOPA
  • They are synthesized in :
  • -Parvocellular neurons in PVN
  • -Arcuat N (except for dopamine=monoamine, they are peptides)
  • Short T1/2
  • →(exert a general influence on the homeostasis of the organism via their effects on the adenohypophysis.)
  • ⇒ normal hypothalamic hypophysiotrophic production is taken up rapidly in the hypophyseal portal blood system, and therefore not seen in the peripheral circulation
  • The posterior lobe of the pituitary (neurohypophysis) is made up of the endings of neurons whose cell bodies reside in the SOP and PVN

Slide 14 #14

  • !!!!Most of the anterior pituitary hormones are under predominantly positive control by hypothalamic releasing hormones; the exception is prolactin, which is under tonic inhibition by dopamine.
  • Hypothalamic releasing hormones regulate the secretion of Ant HPF H.
  • GnRH (+)→ FSH, LH
  • GHRH(+) → GH (STH), SS (-)→ GH (STH)
  • TRH(+) → TSH
  • CRH(+) → ACTH
  • TRH(+), DOPA(-) → PRL
  • !!! Pituitary PRL secretion is primarly regulated by dopamine (HT)→ D2 rec of lactotrophs → (-) PRL secretion
  • Some hypophysiotropic hormones are multifunctional.
  • The hormones of the hypothalamus are secreted episodically and not continuously, and in some cases there is an underlying circadian rhythm.

Physiologic puberty #15

  • Is one stage in the continuing process of growth and development that brings
  • about
  • secondary sexual development,
  • the pubertal growth spurt
  • full development of gonads, external genitalia, internal genitalia and
  • fertility
  • ( the normal age at onset of puberty :girls:8-13 years; boys: 9-14 years)
  • After an interval of childhood quiescence—the juvenile pause-
  • ←the hypothalamic pulse generator increases activity in the peripubertal period,→ increased secretion of HPF gonadotropins and subsequently, gonadal sex steroids
  • It is not clear what triggers the onset of puberty, but stimuli from the cerebral cortex and limbic system via various neurotransmitters, e.g. leptin, kisspeptin, endorphins, catecholamines, and dopamine

Physiologic puberty #16

  • Female changes:
  • Breast development (thelarche) =the first noted sign of puberty, pubic hair development, adrenarche (the secretion of adrenal androgens) , menarche
  • Development of internal and external genitalia
  • Pubertal growth spurt (=the first sign), bone mass acquisition
  • Gynoid body fat disposition
  • Tanner and Marshall.

Physiologic puberty #17

  • Male changes:
  • An increase in the size of the testes = the first sign of normal puberty
  • Development of internal and external genitalia
  • Pubic hair development, facial and thoracic hair development, adrenarche
  • The onset of erections
  • Pubertal growth spurt, rapid acquisition of mineral bone mass
  • Muscle mass development, thickening of voice
  • seborrheic, acne skin
  • Tanner şi Marshall.

Precocious puberty (PP) #18

  • = the appearance of secondary sexual development before the age of 9 years in boys, and 7- 8 years in caucasian girls (6-8 years in African American girls)
  • Classification
  • 1.Central (complete or true) precocious puberty→ the cause is premature activation of the HPT-HPF axis ( spermatogenesis in M and ovulation in F may occur and fertility is possible)( the secondary sexual development is according to genetic sex)
  • 2.Incomplete precocious puberty →premature sexual development in the absence of HPT-HPF maturation ( without gametogenesis!)
  • a. incomplete isosexual precocious puberty( the secondary sexual development is according to genetic sex)
  • in males←: excess of hCG or LH secreted by tumors
  • ← :excess of androgens (eg 21-hydroxylase deficiency)
  • in females ← a source of excessive estrogens
  • b. incomplete contrasexual precocious puberty
  • in males ← excess of estrogens which leads to inappropriate feminization
  • in females ←excess of androgens with inappropriate virilization (eg 21-hydroxylase deficiency)

Central (Complete or true) PP #19

  • Etiology of central (complete or true )PP:
  • constitutional (a familial tendency towards early puberty)
  • CNS disorders such as-tumors, infectious or granulomatous conditions might trigger pathologic forms of precocious puberty
  • idiopathic (in the absence of CNS abnormality, no family history)
  • Clinical features
  • 1. Precocious development of secondary sexual characteristics, internal and external genitalia
  • B2 (Tanner) la ♀
  • G2 (testis.> 2.5 cm (diam.long)) la ♂
  • and/or pubic- axillay haïr P2 in both sexe
  • 2. Increased somatic development, an increase in growth velocity and skeletal maturation;
  • →when unchecked, this rapid epiphyseal development may lead to tall stature during the early phases of the disorder but to short final stature because of early epiphyseal fusion !!
  • This is the paradox of the tall child growing up to become a short adult !!
  • Psychic manifestations
  • 4. Others manifestations according to etiology
  • More commonly found in girls

Investigations #20

  • 1. Hormonology: basal E2/T ↑, FSH ↑, LH ↑ (in the pubertal range; basal LH>0.3U/L indicates the onset of puberty)
  • The diagnostic test= GnRH stimulation test: stimulation with 100 µg GnRH (iv) or GnRH agonist sc→ ↑LH (especially), FSH (pubertal response).
  • The rise of LH after GnRH is used as a diagnostic test to differentiate central precocious puberty from the prepubertal state/peripheral precocity
  • A peak stimulated LH of >∼8 mIU/mL after GnRH and >∼5 IU/L after GnRH agonist are considered indicative of CPP AND
  • No increase in LH and FSH levels after GnRH suggests peripheral precocity.
  • 2. Radiographs (of left wrist and hand) for determination of bone age→ advanced bone age = very effective indicator of precocious puberty
  • 3. Ultrasonography of the ovary and uterus:- uterine size ↑, developing ovarian follicles/ ↑ testicular volume and prostate (♂).
  • 4. Cerebral MRI with contrast or CT scanning ( → (to rule out a CNS tumor/other pathological processes) –mandatory in ♂ and ♀ < the age of 6)

Treatment (of PP either idiopathic or due to a CNS lesion)- #21

  • Objectives: to suppress sexual maturation and decrease growth rate and skeletal maturation
  • GnRH agonists: chronic administration of highly potent and long-acting analogs of GnRH has been shown to downregulate GnRH receptors and reduce HPF gland response to GnRH, thereby causing ↓ secretion of FSH and LH and sex steroids and rapidly stopping the progression of signs of sexual precocity
  • Triptorelin (DIPHERELINE) 3.75 mg/vial - cca 1 f/month i.m./ or Diphereline PR 11.25 mg every 3 months
  • other depot preparations-every 3 months/ implantable pellets left in place for 1-2 years

Delayed puberty or absent puberty (sexual infantilism) #22

  • Definition: Any girl of 13 or boy of 14 years of age without signs of pubertal development falls more than 2.5 DS above the mean and is considered to have delayed puberty.
  • Classification of delayed puberty
  • The challenging task for the examining physician is to decide which patients are constitutionally delayed and which have organic disease
Constitutional delay in growth and adolescence
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Kallmann syndrome (KAL1 gene which encodes for anosmin- genetic form of isolated gonadotropin deficiency+hyposmia or anosmia) Multiple pituitary hormonal deficiency Tumors, trauma, irradiation, congenital disorders of the hypothalamus or pituitary
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: Klinefelter syndrome/other forms of primary testicular failure Turner syndrome/other forms of primary ovarian failure

Constitutional delay in growth and adolescence #23

  • Definition=A patient with delayed onset of secondary sexual development, whose stature is shorter than that of age-matched peers but who consistently maintains a normal growth velocity for bone age and whose skeletal development is delayed more than 2 SD from the mean
  • More common in boys than girls
  • The subject is usually thin as well; adrenarche=delayed
  • A family history
  • !!! LH response to exogeneous GnRH or GnRh agonist is pubertal
  • Treatment: observation/reassurance –psychologic support
  • The challenging task for the examining physician is to decide which patients are constitutionally delayed and which have organic disease

The pituitary gland comprises: #24

  • -the predominant anterior lobe
  • -the posterior lobe
  • -a vestigial intermediate lobe
  • The pituitary gland
  • The adult pituitary weighs app 500-900 mg and measures about 13/6-9/9 mm (transverse/vertical/AP diameter, of which the anterior lobe constitutes two-thirds

The anatomic relationships #25

  • The pituitary gland lies at the base of the skull -sell turcica (“Turkish saddle”). The sella turcica forms the thin bony roof of the sphenoid sinus (ant-inf). The gland is surrounded by dura , and the roof is formed by a reflection of dura attached to the clinoid processes, the diaphragma sellae (sup). The arachnoid membrane and, therefore, cerebrospinal fluid are prevented from entering the sella turcica by the diaphragma sellae. The pituitary stalk and its blood vessels pass through an opening in this diaphragm.
  • the anterior clinoid processes
  • the posterior clinoid processes
  • Dura

Slide 26 #26

  • The lateral walls of the gland are in direct apposition to the cavernous sinuses (lateral) and separated from them by dural membranes; the cavernous sinuses are traversed by the III, IV, VI cranial nerves, the ophtalmic branch of Vth cranial nerve and internal carotid arteries. The optic chiasm (sup) lies 5-10 mm above the diaphragma sellae and anterior to the stalk

ADENOHYPOPHYSIS (THE ANTERIOR PITUITARY) #27

  • → originates from Rathke pouch, an ectodermal evagination of the oropharynx, and migrates to join the neurohypophysis

Major adenohypophysial hormones and their cellular sources #28

  • ACTH-MSH
  • GH
  • FSH
  • LH
  • TSH
  • PRL
  • Immunocytochemical and EM techniques permit classification of cells by their specific secretory products:
  • -somatotrophs (GH-secreting cells) (acidophil)
  • -gonadotrops (FSH, LH-secreting cells)
  • -thyrotrops (TSH-secreting cells)
  • -corticotrophs (ACTH-secreting cells)
  • -lactotrops ( PRL-secreting cells) (acidophil)

Major adenohypophysial hormones and their main functions #29

  • GH – stimulates the production of IGF-1 (the mediator of the indirect actions of GH); also exerts direct actions on growth and metabolism
  • PRL – stimulation of milk production (protein and lactose synthesis, water excretion, and sodium retention); inhibits gonadotropins secretion
  • ACTH – stimulation of Gc (glucocorticoids) and sex steroids in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex, inducing hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the adrenal cortex
  • TSH – stimulation of all aspects of thyroid gland function: h. synthesis, secretion; hyperplasia, hypertrophy and vascularization of thyroid gl
  • LH – Females: stimulates steroid h (androgens) synthesis in theca interna cells, lutein and hilar cells; ovulation induction; promotes luteinization, maintains the corpus luteum, stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone
  • Males: stimulates steroid h production in Leydig cells
  • FSH – Females: targets the granulosa cells to promote follicular development; stimulates aromatase expression and inhibin secretion
  • Males: targets the Sertoli cells to promote spermatogenesis and to stimulate inhibin secretion
  • !Maturation of spematozoa, however, requires both LH and FSH!

THE PITUITARY TUMORAL SYNDROME (Pituitary Mass Effects) #30

  • Definition
  • The sum of symptoms and signs caused by an expanding pituitary mass in the sella turcica or the suprasellar space ( the space between HPT-HPF)

The pituitary tumoral syndrome (sellar and parasellar masses)– etiology #31

  • 1. PITUITARY ADENOMAS (over 95% of cases)-benign; most are monoclonal; ←pituitary gland cells
  • classification: according to the size of the tumor
  • microadenomas: intrasellar adenomas < 1 cm in diameter without sellar enlargement or extrasellar extension
  • macroadenomas : >1cm and causing generalized sellar enlargement
  • according to the state of h secretion
  • nonfunctional pituitary adenoma
  • functional pituitary adenomas: prolactinomas eg.
  • 2. CRANIOPHRYNGIOMA
  • Craniopharyngiomas are thought to originate from metaplasia of remnant epithelial cell rests in Rathke pouch during development. They appear as intra- and/or suprasellar masses with cystic and/or solid components and calcifications.
  • (most common in children, adolescents, and young adults).
  • 3. METASTATIC LESIONS ( carcinomas that metastasize to the HPF include breast, lung and gastrointestinal cancers)
  • 4. MISCELLANEOUS LESIONS:SARCOIDOSIS, HISTIOCYTOSIS X,LYMPHOMAS, LYMPHOCYTIC HYPOPHYSITIS, PITUITARY ABSCESSES, MENINGIOMA, CYSTS

Clinical features #32

  • 1. NEUROLOGICAL SIGNS
  • 2. OPHTALMOLOGICAL SIGNS
  • 3. ENDOCRINO-METABOLIC SIGNS
  • (4. IMAGING STUDIES)

Neurological signs #33

  • Headache –the major symptom– with some specific characteristics- frontal, fronto-parietal or retro-orbital localization ; none or only partial amelioration with the usual pain killers drugs administration; progressive
  • ! the substratum of headache= diaphragmatic distortions or dural impingement (stretching of the dural plate ) by a tumoral mass having an anterior –superior evolution
  • the evolution of pituitary masses towards the hypothalamus →disorders of consciousness, behavior, thirst, appetite and temperature regulation: hyperphagia and weight gain, loss of thirst sensation etc (=the hypothalamic syndrome); + hypopituitarism and central diabetes insipidus
  • Large pituitary lesions may extend laterally into the cavernous sinus, compromising the function of the third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerve : → diplopia, palpebral ptosis, palsy of cranial nerves III, IV, VI, ↓ facial sensation , and internal carotid artery compression or cavernous sinus thrombosis
  • Inferior extension – leading to eroding of the bony sellar floor and its extension into the sphenoid sinus
  • Very large tumors with both suprasellar and parasellar extension→ to features of ↑intracranial pressure ( ICP ): severe, persistent headache, vomiting, seizures, pulse↓, focal neurology, papilloedema
  • = neurosurgery emergencies

Ophtalmological signs #34

  • impinging upon the optic chiasm or optic tract results in optic –chiasmatic syndrom;
  • Bitemporal hemianopia= the classic visual field defect
  • Visual fields are assessed by bedside confrontational testing, Goldman perimetry and automed quantitative perimetry
  • OD
  • OS

  • The optic chiasm and optic tracts are particularly vulnerable to compression by expanding pituitary masses, and expanding pituitary tumors affect mostly the chiasma.
  • A visual field is the entire area seen by an eye when its gaze is fixed on a central point; the circumference of the circle is 90 from the line of gaze as measured from the corneal surface

VF #35

  • R
  • Oc
  • OT
  • -bitemporal visual loss in the superior field portion ( bitemporal sup quadrantanopia)
  • -bitemporal hemianopia
  • = impingement upon the optic chiasma
  • -homonymous right hemianopia h
  • = pressure on the left optic tract
  • Nasal
  • Temporal
  • Temporal
  • Because of the anatomy of the chiasma, pressure from below affects temporal visual fields, starting superiorly (← pressure on the inferior crossing chiasmatic fibres which leads to bitemporal visual loss, in the superior field portions= bitemporal sup quadrantanopia) and ultimately extending to entire temporal field loss= bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Tumor evolution towards an optic tract (bandelet ) leads to visual loss in the temporal field of one ocular globe and respectively the nasal field of the other ocular globe = homonymous contralateral hemianopia

Ophtalmological signs #36

  • Rarely, decreased visual acuity, pupillary abnormalities, optic atrophy, papilledema, cranial nerve palsies, and nystagmus may be encountered.
  • = OPTOCHIASMATIC sdr= neurosurgery emergencies

Endocrine and metabolic signs #37

  • Include symptoms and signs of – A. hormone hypersecretion and/or
  • B. hypopituitarism← caused by tumoral local pressure on the healthy pituitary gland or by the hormonal excess (for example: ↑PRL→ LH, FSH↓)
  • PITUITARY HYPERSECRETION
  • CLINICAL FEATURES ARE ACCORDING TO THE HORMONAL HYPERSECRETION TYPE
  • PROLACTINOMA - the most common type, accounting for about 60% of
  • primary pituitary tumors leads to amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility in F
  • and ↓ libido, impotence, male infertility in M
  • GH/GH+PRL SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMAS– 10-15% -gigantism/ acromegaly
  • ACTH SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMAS – 5%- Cushing disease
  • TSH-SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMAS – 1%-HYPERTHYROIDISM WITH GOITER
  • (FSH, LH) GONADOTROPIN-SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA – 1-2%- usual large cromophobe adenomas presenting with visual impairment, hypopituitarism / rarely ovarian hyperstimulation
  • NONFUNCTIONAL PITUITARY ADENOMAS - 28%

Endocrine and metabolic signs #38

  • B. PITUITARY INSUFFICIENCY
  • Pituitary failure (hypopituitarism) refers to either partial or complete deficiency of pituitary hormones
  • ← as a consequence of anterior pituitary gland distruction
Main manifestations of hypopituitarism
Hormone deficiencyClinical features
GHChildren;short stature/ adults: reduced exercise capacity, ↓lean body mass, ↑body fat, impaired psychological well-being,↑ cardiovascular risk
LH/FSH♀:oligo/amenorrhea, anovulatory cycles, loss of axillary and pubic hair, osteoporosis ♂: erectile dysfunction, ↓libido, testicular atrophy, loss of sexual hair, osteoporosis
TSHAs in primary hypothyroidism, except lack of goiter ( see chapter)
ACTHAs in Addison’ s disease (primary ACI) except lack of hyperpigmentation, hyperkalaemia
ProlactinFailure of lactation
ADHPolyuria and polydipsia

Imaging studies #39

  •  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) currently provides the optimal imaging of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus and readily shows any significant pituitary mass.
  •  Computed tomography (CT) scans may still be useful in demonstrating calcification in tumors (e.g. craniopharyngiomas) and hyperostosis in association with meningiomas or evidence of bone destruction as well as for discovery of hemorrhagic lesions
  •  Plain skull radiography (or Radiography of the sella turcica) may show evidence of pituitary fossa enlargement (however, it does not “see” the pituitary gland or a pituitary tumor) but has been superseded by MRI.

Slide 40 #40

  • Gadolinium-enhanced MR images are shown of the pituitary gland. A and B: Coronal and sagittal images show the normal, uniformly enhancing pituitary stalk and pituitary gland.
  • High-resolution T1-weighted sections in the coronal and sagittal planes both before and after administration of IV gadolinium compounds for contrast distinguish most pituitary masses.
  • The post pituitary appears on MRI as a high-signal-intensity structure, the “post pituitary bright spot” (due to neurosecretory granules), which is absent in patients with DI.

Slide 41 #41

  • Gadolinium-enhanced MR images are shown of the pituitary gland. A and B: Coronal and sagittal images show the normal, uniformly enhancing pituitary stalk and pituitary gland.
  • C: A pituitary microadenoma appears as a low-intensity lesion in the inferior aspect of the right lobe of the gland (arrow).
  • D: The pituitary microadenoma appears as a low-intensity lesion between the left lobe of the pituitary and the left cavernous sinus (arrow).
  • • Microadenomas: (2-9mm) - On T1-weighted images they appear as a low-signal intensity lesions than the remainder of the normal gland and do not usually enhances with gadolinium ( hypodense); sometimes difficult to be visualized. Contrast enhancement, asymmetry of the gland (a unilateral convex superior gland margin), or stalk position (e.g., deviation of the pituitary stalk toward the side opposite the adenoma) can be helpful in demonstrating their presence.

Slide 42 #42

  • A. The coronal MR image shows a large nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma (arrows) with pronounced suprasellar extension and chiasmal compression.
  • B: A sagittal MR image of another large pituitary adenoma shows spontaneous hemorrhage within the suprasellar portion of the adenoma (arrows).
  • • Macroadenomas: >10mm in diameter- readily visualized with MRI scans, and the scan will also define the adjacent structures and the degree of extension of the lesion → compression of the normal pituitary and distortion of the pituitary stalk, compression and upward displacement of the optic chiasma (suprasellar extension), cavernous sinus invasion (lateral extension), or sphenoid sinus extension;
  • !Contrary to microadenomas, macroadenomas, which are significantly more vascular, have a higher affinity to gadolinium.

Management of pituitary masses #43

  • THE GOALS OF THERAPY:
  • Excision of mass lesions causing pressure effects
  • suppression/ correction of hormonal hypersecretion
  • Preserving the normal secretion of anterior pituitary hormones ( or correcting their insufficiency)
  • MODES OF THERAPY
  • 1.SURGERY
  • 2. RADIOTHERAPY
  • 3. DRUGS: to suppress hypersecretion by the adenoma or its growth.

TREATMENT #44

  • 1. SURGICAL TREATMENT
  • TRANSSPHENOIDAL SURGERY= is the procedure of choice ( with selective resection of the lesion)
  • Pituitary microadenoma-complete removal
  • Pituitary macroadenoma- partial excision
  • ↓ morbidity and mortality
  • Major complications include postoperative hemorrhage, cerebrospinal fluid leak, meningitis, and visual impairment, transitory diabetes insipidus< 5% of patients
  • TRANSFRONTAL/ TRANSPARIETAL CRANIOTOMY
  • Is required only for the rare invasive suprasellar mass extending into the frontal or middle cranial fossa or optic nerves or having extensive posterior clivus invasion
  • !Accompanied more frequently by major neurological, endocrine complications ( DI, pituitary failure), visual impairments

Treatment #45

  • 2. RADIOTHERAPY
  • Is usual reserved for-residual mass effect or recurrent tumors following surgery, when surgery for a compressive mass is contraindicated, or persistent hormone hypersecretion after surgery is noted
  • Possibilities:
  • Conventional irradiation using high-energy sources (total dose = 10000-12000 Rads in 2-3 sessions, each divided in daily doses of 180-200 Rads)(in Ro in the past)
  • Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is usually employed as an adjuvant treatment in patients with residual or recurrent tumors following surgery.
  • Gamma knife radiosurgery (GK)- (the most frequently used SRS technique worldwide) utilizes stereotactic CT-guided cobalt 60-gamma radiation to deliver high radiation doses to a narrowly focused area, while minimizing the mass of normal brain exposed to radiation (an adequate distance of the pituitary mass from the OC is needed); GK is usually given in single fraction
  • The GK system consists of an array of 192 or 201 sources of cobalt-60 that align with an inner collimator to direct the resulting photon beams delivered by the decay of Cobalt 60 (gamma rays). All the beams converge at a single point called the isocenter
  • Fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy (fSRT) (the total dose of stereotactic radiation is divided into several smaller doses of radiation, on separate days of treatment; typically, this consists of 2 to 5 treatments)
  • Side effects: visual damage (damage to the optic nerve or chiasma), hypopituitarism (is common, and the incidence increases with time following radiotherapy—about 50% to 60% at 5 to 10 years), seizures, cognitive disorders, radionecrosis of brain tissue

A margin dose of 12–15 Gy is used for nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas; #46

  • Higher margin doses (up to 20–30 Gy) are used for functional adenomas;
  • GK SRS is safe and provides tumor control in >90% patients with recurrent or residual nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas;
  • Risks of visual dysfunction, or neurological deficit appear to be quite low;
  • Delayed pituitary insufficiency can be expected in 30–40% patients;
  • The endocrine remission response to SRS is best with ACTH producing tumors, followed by GH producing tumors, with prolactinoma having the poorest response.

Treatment #47

  • 3. MEDICAL TREATMENT
  • Suppression of hormone hypersecretion became feasible with the availability of :
  • bromocriptine or cabergoline, two dopamine agonists that suppress both PRL and tumor growth in patients with prolactinomas (used also in acromegaly, and sometimes used also in nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas),
  • somatostatin analogs, useful in the therapy of acromegaly, some TSH-secreting adenomas, Cushing’s disease (see later)
  • Replacement treatment of the anterior pituitary gland insufficiency

NEUROHYPOPHYSIS (Posterior Pituitary) #48

THE HORMONES OF NEUROHYPOPHYSIS #49

  • All defined pathophysiology of the posterior pituitary is related to the function of vasopressin rather than oxytocin.
  • Oxytocin
  • (+) contraction of the myoepithelial cells of the mammary ducts and the ejection of milk
  • (+) uterine contraction during labor
  • Vasopressin
  • = the water-retaining hormone in all mammals and along with thirst is the primary regulator of osmolality.
  • ADH (AVP, arginine vasopressin)-stimuli for ADH secretion:
  • (+): ↓ blood volume, ↑plasma osmolality , exercise, nicotin, angiotensin II, high temperature
  • (-): low temperature ( coldness), alcohol
  • effect: the major renal effect of ADH is to increase water reabsortion at the collecting renal duct level
  • ADH =important regulator of-plasma osmolality
  • -water balance
  • -arterial pressure

Diabetes insipidus (DI) #50

  • = clinical features are the result of
  • Failure to secrete adequate quantities of ADH or
  • Failure of the kidney to respond to circulating ADH
  • Classification of DI
  • CENTRAL DI
  • NEPHROGENIC DI
  • Transitory DI
  • Permanent DI
  • Partial
  • complete

Etiology of DI #51

  • CENTRAL DIABETES INSIPIDUS
  • Craniopharyngiomas (the most common of solid tumor to produce DI), pituitary infiltration by metastases, suprasellar pinealomas, germinomas in children
  • surgery in the hypothalamic, pituitary stalk area
  • head trauma
  • infiltrative disorders: sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, limphomas
  • infections: meningitis, meningoencephalities
  • autoimmune
  • DIDMOAD syndrome=DI+ DM+ optic atrophy+ deafness
  • idiopathic
  • NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS
  • Acquired: chronic renal disease: any renal disease that interferes with collecting duct or medullary function, eg, chronic pyelonephritis, toxic nephritis, postobstructive uropathy
  • hypokalemia, hypercalcemia
  • drugs: lithyum, demeclocycline
  • Familial:
  • X-linked recessive—vasopressin receptor gene or
  • autosomal recessive—aquaporin-2 gene.

Clinical features of DI #52

  • • Adults—polyuria, nocturia, and thirst, polydipsia
  • • Children—polyuria, enuresis, and failure to thrive.
  • Rarely: acute dehydration characterized by arterial hypotension, shock and coma.

Diagnosis of type of DI #53

  • Confirm large urine output (>3L/day) (with low urinary density (the urine specific gravity)<1005)
  • 2. Exclude diabetes mellitus and renal failure (osmotic diuresis) as well as other causes of polyuria (hypokalaemia and hypercalcaemia: check electrolytes)
  • 3. Dehydration test ( water deprivation):
  • no fluids for 12-18 hours; measure body W, TA, pulse, urine flow and urine specific gravity each hour; urine and plasma osmolality
  • ! In DI the urine flow remains increased, while urine specific gravity is less than 1005; the patient becomes dehydrated.
  • serum osmolality rises above normal without adequate concentration of urine osmolality (i.e. serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality <600 (or even <400) mOsm/kg or urine density <1011).
  • In Primary polydipsia- urine osmolality <600 mOsm/kg but > 400 mOsm/kg or urine density >1011 but <1017
  • There are no difficulties in diagnosing sever central or nephrogenic DI.
  • The challenging task for the clinician is to distinguish cranial diabetes -the partial form from primary polydipsia.

Diagnosis of type of DI #54

  • 4. Direct measurement of ADH (AVP) concentrations: levels are ↓in central DI and↑ in nephrogenic DI (unstable)
  • Copeptin assay (a glycopeptide comprising the C-terminal part of the AVP prohormone)
  • Vasopressin test:
  • - once the diagnosis of DI is established, the ADH-insensitive (nephrogenic) disease must be distinguished from the ADH-sensitive (central) form;
  • - this is done by giving 5 units of vasopressin parenterally or 2 µg of desmopressin (Deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin), the synthetic analogue of ADH either through intravenous or intramuscular route and then measuring urinary flow and D for 2 more hours:
  • a) in central DI : urinary flow↓ and urinary D and osmolality ↑
  • b) in nephrogenic DI: urinary flow remains ↑ and urinary D and osmolality↓
  • In specialized units, measurement of copeptin during hypertonic saline infusion should be regarded as gold standard
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537591/table/diagn-diabet-insip.T.hypertonic_saline_i/

Diagnosis of type of DI #55

  • Investigation of the cause
  • MRI head:
  • • Looking for tumours (e.g. hypothalamic, pineal, or infiltration).
  • • May demonstrate loss of bright spot of posterior pituitary gland.
  • Abdominal ultrasound, intravenous urography: for the renal pathology

DI -Differential diagnosis of polyuria #56

  • Primary polydipsia (potomania)
  • Dehydration test: (+)- urine osmolality ( and density) will rise
  • It involves greatly increased drinking in excess of 5 liters/day, leading to dilution of the extracellular fluid, inhibition of ADH secretion, and water diuresis (there may be impaired renal effectiveness because of washout of solute and, therefore, reduced urine-concentrating ability).
  • It is a disorder of thirst that is either due to psychogenic causes or to altered osmotic and nonosmotic regulation of thirst (←intracranial etiology)
  • Other causes of polyuria syndrome
  • -renal chronic failure ( polyuric phase), DM, hypercalcemia, hypo K+

Treatment-DI #57

  • CENTRAL DIABETES INSIPIDUS
  • Hormonal treatment of substitution:
  • Desmopressin acetate
  • =Vasopressin analogue, acting predominantly on the V2 receptors in the kidney
  • Drug may be administered in divided doses, orally Minirin ®(100–1,000 micrograms/day), intranasally (10–40 micrograms/day), parenterally (SC, IV, IM) (0.1–2 micrograms/day) or sublingually.- Minirin melt ®60-120 µg 3times/day sublingual
  • Etiologic treatment: the underlying disorder should be treated if possible
  • NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS
  • • Correction of underlying cause (metabolic or drugs).
  • • Maintenance of adequate fluid input.
  • • High doses of desmopressin (e.g. up to 5 micrograms IM) can be effective.
  • • Thiazide diuretics- Hydroclorothiazide (NEFRIX) 25-50 mg/day+ low sodium diet
